{
  "augmentations": [
    {
      "gap": "G1",
      "title": "Projection interpretation of dot product and work",
      "content": "The dot product is best seen as projection. If a force F makes an angle θ with a displacement d, the component of F along d is F cos θ. Work is that component multiplied by the displacement magnitude: W = (F cos θ)d = F d cos θ = F·d. Geometrically, project F onto d; the length of the projection is F cos θ. If θ = 0, W = Fd; if θ = 90°, W = 0; if θ > 90°, W is negative. Example: a 10 N force acting at 60° to a 4 m displacement does W = 10 × 4 × 0.5 = 20 J. A 10 N force opposite to a 4 m displacement does W = -40 J.",
      "level": "within",
      "provenance": "standard_knowledge",
      "sources": [],
      "textbook_note": "Keeps the textbook's W = F·d and F d cos θ; makes the projection reason explicit."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G2",
      "title": "Effort is not always mechanical work",
      "content": "In physics, work requires a displacement of the point where the force acts and a force component along that displacement. Holding a 50 N load stationary for 10 s does no mechanical work because d = 0, even though muscles consume chemical energy and produce heat. Pushing a rigid wall with 100 N for 5 s also does no work if the wall does not move. Carrying a 5 kg bag horizontally at constant height: the hand's upward force is about 49 N and the displacement is horizontal, so θ = 90° and the work by that force is 0 J; lifting the bag 1 m does W = mgh = 5 × 9.8 × 1 = 49 J. The correction is: tiredness or effort is not the same as mechanical work; only F·d counts.",
      "level": "within",
      "provenance": "standard_knowledge",
      "sources": [],
      "textbook_note": "Clarifies the textbook's zero-work conditions in T6 and the skidding-cycle example in T7."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G3",
      "title": "Why kinetic energy has the factor 1/2",
      "content": "The factor 1/2 is not arbitrary. For a constant force, v^2 - u^2 = 2as. Multiplying by m/2 gives 1/2 m v^2 - 1/2 m u^2 = mas = Fs. For a variable force, use F = ma = m dv/dt and dW = F dx = m v dv/dt dx = m v dv. Integrating gives K = 1/2 m v^2. Thus kinetic energy is the quantity whose change equals the accumulated work. Example: a 2 kg object accelerated from rest to 3 m/s has K = 1/2 × 2 × 3^2 = 9 J; a 3 N force over 3 m also gives W = 9 J.",
      "level": "within",
      "provenance": "standard_knowledge",
      "sources": [],
      "textbook_note": "Explains the textbook's motivation from v^2-u^2=2as and the definition K=1/2 mv^2."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G4",
      "title": "Calculus prerequisite: integral as area and chain rule",
      "content": "Before variable-force work, review two calculus ideas. First, a definite integral ∫_xi^xf F(x) dx is the signed area under the force-displacement graph. Area above the x-axis is positive, below is negative, and the unit is N m = J. Example: F(x)=2x N from x=0 to 3 m gives ∫0^3 2x dx = [x^2]_0^3 = 9 J. Second, for constant mass, dK/dt = d(1/2 m v^2)/dt = m v dv/dt by the chain rule. Since v = dx/dt, dK/dt = F v when F = ma, so dK = F dx. This is the bridge from power P = F·v to the work-energy theorem.",
      "level": "within",
      "provenance": "standard_knowledge",
      "sources": [],
      "textbook_note": "Supplies the calculus background used in T10 and T11 without changing the textbook's notation."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G5",
      "title": "From small-step sum to definite integral",
      "content": "To see W = ∫ F dx as a method, split the displacement from xi to xf into small pieces Δx_i. Over each small piece, approximate the force as constant: ΔW_i ≈ F(x_i) Δx_i. The total work is the sum Σ F(x_i) Δx_i. As the pieces become smaller and more numerous, the sum approaches the definite integral ∫_xi^xf F(x) dx. The same limiting idea gives dK = F dx for each small step, and summing/integrating gives Kf - Ki = ∫ F dx. Example: for F=2x N from 0 to 3 m, a coarse midpoint sum with Δx=1 m gives 2(0.5)(1)+2(1.5)(1)+2(2.5)(1)=10 J; the exact integral is 9 J, and the sum improves as Δx decreases.",
      "level": "within",
      "provenance": "standard_knowledge",
      "sources": [],
      "textbook_note": "Fills the skipped limiting step in T10 and T11 while keeping the textbook's integral form."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G6",
      "title": "Meaning of the minus sign in F = -dV/dx",
      "content": "The minus sign means a conservative force points toward lower potential energy. If V increases with x, dV/dx is positive, so F is negative: the force acts toward decreasing x. For gravity near Earth, take h upward, V(h)=mgh, dV/dh=g, so F_h=-mg, i.e. downward. For a spring, V(x)=1/2 kx^2, dV/dx=kx, so F=-kx, restoring toward x=0. Equivalently, dV = -F dx: when the force and displacement are in the same direction, potential energy decreases; when you move against the force, potential energy increases. Example: lifting a 2 kg mass by 1 m increases V by 19.6 J, while gravity does -19.6 J of work.",
      "level": "within",
      "provenance": "standard_knowledge",
      "sources": [],
      "textbook_note": "Keeps the textbook's F = -dV/dx and makes the sign physically meaningful for gravity and springs."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G7",
      "title": "Deriving spring potential energy from variable force",
      "content": "A spring force is not constant: F_s = -kx. To stretch it slowly from x=0 to x, an external agent applies +kx. The work done by the external agent is the area under the F-x graph, a triangle with base x and height kx: W_ext = 1/2 (kx)(x) = 1/2 kx^2. In integral form, W_ext = ∫_0^x kx' dx' = 1/2 kx^2. The spring force does the negative of this work, so the stored potential energy is V(x)=1/2 kx^2, with V(0)=0. Example: k=200 N/m, x=0.10 m gives V=1/2 × 200 × 0.10^2 = 1.0 J; the average external force is 10 N over 0.10 m, also 1.0 J.",
      "level": "within",
      "provenance": "standard_knowledge",
      "sources": [],
      "textbook_note": "Fills the skipped average-force/integral step in T16 and keeps the textbook's zero at equilibrium."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G8",
      "title": "Friction converts mechanical energy, it does not destroy it",
      "content": "A common misconception is that friction destroys energy. In fact, friction converts mechanical energy into internal thermal energy, sound, and deformation. For a block sliding with a friction force of 5 N over 3 m, W_f = -15 J; the block's kinetic energy decreases by 15 J, and about 15 J appears as heat in the block and surface. In a skidding car, kinetic energy becomes heat in tires and road. In an inelastic collision, the decrease in kinetic energy becomes deformation, heat, and sound. The textbook relation Ef - Ei = W_nc is therefore not a loss of total energy: if W_nc is negative, mechanical energy decreases, but total energy including thermal energy is conserved.",
      "level": "within",
      "provenance": "standard_knowledge",
      "sources": [],
      "textbook_note": "Refines T14 and T18 by distinguishing mechanical energy from total energy while keeping Ef - Ei = W_nc."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G9",
      "title": "Relative-speed relation in 1D elastic collisions",
      "content": "The algebraic key is that for a 1D elastic collision the relative speed reverses: v1i - v2i = v2f - v1f, or v1i - v2i = -(v1f - v2f). This follows from combining momentum conservation with kinetic-energy conservation. If m2 is initially at rest, v2i=0, so v1i = v2f - v1f. Combine this with momentum conservation m1 v1i = m1 v1f + m2 v2f to solve linearly: v1f = ((m1 - m2)/(m1 + m2)) v1i and v2f = (2m1/(m1 + m2)) v1i. Example: equal masses, v1i=4 m/s, v2i=0 gives v1f=0 and v2f=4 m/s; the moving ball stops and the stationary ball moves off with the original speed.",
      "level": "within",
      "provenance": "standard_knowledge",
      "sources": [],
      "textbook_note": "Supplies the missing intermediate relation in T22 and keeps the textbook's final formulas."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G10",
      "title": "Vector-triangle picture for equal-mass glancing collisions",
      "content": "For two equal masses with one initially at rest, momentum conservation gives m v_i = m v1f + m v2f, so v_i = v1f + v2f as a vector equation. Elastic energy conservation gives 1/2 m v_i^2 = 1/2 m v1f^2 + 1/2 m v2f^2, so v_i^2 = v1f^2 + v2f^2. These two equations say that the two final velocity vectors are the legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the initial velocity vector. Therefore v1f and v2f are perpendicular. A useful drawing is: draw the initial momentum as the hypotenuse, then draw the two final momenta as the two sides meeting at a right angle. If one final velocity makes an angle θ with the initial direction on one side, the other makes 90° - θ with the initial direction on the opposite side.",
      "level": "within",
      "provenance": "standard_knowledge",
      "sources": [],
      "textbook_note": "Adds a visual interpretation to the algebraic proof in T25 and the 2D equations in T24."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G11",
      "title": "Real crash context for the car-spring model",
      "content": "The textbook car-spring example is an ideal Hooke's-law model: the force is linear, the energy is stored elastically, and the car can rebound. A real frontal crash is different. A 1500 kg car at 50 km/h has speed 13.9 m/s and kinetic energy K = 1/2 m v^2 ≈ 1.45 × 10^5 J = 145 kJ. In a full frontal crash, essentially all of this energy must be dissipated. Crumple zones are the primary absorbers; a commonly cited conservative figure is that the front crumple zone absorbs about 25% of the impact energy, about 36 kJ at 50 km/h, though the actual share can be higher depending on vehicle design. The NHTSA full-frontal rigid-barrier test at 35 mph, about 56 km/h, corresponds to about 181 kJ for the same 1500 kg car. A real force-displacement curve has a peak force followed by a plateau over a crush distance of roughly 0.5 to 1 m; the work is the area under that curve, and the energy becomes heat and permanent deformation rather than recoverable spring energy. If 36 kJ is absorbed over 0.7 m, the average force associated with that portion is about 50 kN, corresponding to an average deceleration of about 3 to 4 g for that portion; the total crash deceleration depends on all energy-absorbing structures. Historically, the crumple-zone concept was developed in 20th-century automotive safety research, notably by György Barényi.",
      "level": "extension",
      "provenance": "web",
      "sources": [
        "https://www.nhtsa.gov/ratings",
        "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crumple_zone",
        "https://suncollision.com/why-are-cars-designed-to-crumple-in-the-front-during-collisions"
      ],
      "textbook_note": "Keeps the textbook's ideal spring model and energy-conservation calculation; presents real crash behaviour as an extension and refinement."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G12",
      "title": "Reactor context for neutron moderation",
      "content": "The NCERT neutron example is a clean elastic-collision application. In real reactors, fission neutrons are fast, with mean energy about 2 MeV and speed about 20,000 km/s. They must be slowed to thermal energies, about 0.025 eV and 2.2 km/s, because U-235 fission is much more probable with slow neutrons. This is an energy reduction by about 8 × 10^7 and a speed reduction by about 10,000. Light nuclei are effective because in a head-on elastic collision the maximum fraction of the neutron's kinetic energy transferred to a stationary nucleus of mass number A is 4A/(1+A)^2: hydrogen A=1 gives 100%, deuterium A=2 gives about 89%, carbon A=12 gives about 28%, while U-235 gives only about 1.7%. Average slowing requires many collisions: roughly 17 to 18 for hydrogen, 25 to 30 for deuterium, and 90 to 115 for graphite. Common moderators are light water, heavy water, and graphite. Light water is the most common, about 75% of reactors, but ordinary hydrogen absorbs some neutrons, so light-water reactors usually need enriched uranium, about 3.5 to 5% U-235. Heavy water, about 5% of reactors, absorbs fewer neutrons and can use natural uranium, about 0.7% U-235, as in CANDU reactors. Graphite, about 20% of reactors, also has low absorption and can use natural uranium, as in RBMK and Magnox/AGR reactors. The kinetic energy lost by neutrons becomes heat in the moderator and is removed by the coolant.",
      "level": "extension",
      "provenance": "web",
      "sources": [
        "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_moderator",
        "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_temperature",
        "https://nucleus.iaea.org/sites/graphiteknowledgebase/wiki/Wiki%20Pages/Nuclear%20Properties.aspx",
        "https://world-nuclear.org/information-library/nuclear-power-reactors/overview/nuclear-power-reactors"
      ],
      "textbook_note": "Keeps the NCERT neutron-moderation example; adds reactor design context as an extension."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G13",
      "title": "Limitation of V = mgh",
      "content": "The formula V = mgh is the near-Earth, constant-g approximation. It is valid when the height change h is small compared with Earth's radius, so g can be treated as 9.8 m/s^2. Example: a 1 kg mass raised 10 m gains 98 J. For large altitude changes, g decreases with distance from Earth's centre, and the more general gravitational potential energy is U = -GMm/r, which is treated in Chapter 7. For example, at 1000 km above Earth's surface g is noticeably smaller than 9.8 m/s^2, so mgh is no longer a good estimate for a satellite. In this chapter, keep the textbook's mgh for everyday heights and flag it as a local approximation.",
      "level": "within",
      "provenance": "standard_knowledge",
      "sources": [],
      "textbook_note": "Keeps the textbook's near-surface V=mgh and explicitly marks its domain of validity."
    },
    {
      "gap": "G14",
      "title": "Kinetic energy depends on the inertial frame",
      "content": "Kinetic energy K = 1/2 m v^2 is not an absolute number; it depends on the inertial frame because v depends on the frame. A 1 kg ball moving at 2 m/s in the lab frame has K = 2 J, but in a frame moving with the ball its K = 0. The work-energy theorem remains valid in any inertial frame if the work and kinetic energy are both computed in that same frame. In collision problems, choose one inertial frame, usually the lab frame or the centre-of-mass frame, and use it consistently. Example: for a 1 kg ball at 4 m/s colliding elastically with an identical stationary ball, the lab-frame kinetic energy is 8 J before and after; in the centre-of-mass frame the two balls have speeds 2 m/s before and 2 m/s after, with total kinetic energy 4 J. Mixing frames, for example using lab-frame velocities with centre-of-mass work, gives incorrect energy balances.",
      "level": "extension",
      "provenance": "standard_knowledge",
      "sources": [],
      "textbook_note": "Does not change the textbook's K=1/2 mv^2; adds a frame-consistency caution for collisions and work-energy calculations."
    }
  ]
}

G1:
title: "Projection interpretation of dot product and work"
content: "The dot product is best seen as projection. If a force F makes an angle θ with a displacement d, the component of F along d is F cos θ. Work is that component multiplied by the displacement magnitude: W = (F cos θ)d = F d cos θ = F·d. Geometrically, project F onto d; the length of the projection is F cos θ. If θ = 0, W = Fd; if θ = 90°, W = 0; if θ > 90°, W is negative. Example: a 10 N force acting at 60° to a 4 m displacement does W = 10 × 4 × 0.5 = 20 J. A 10 N force opposite to a 4 m displacement does W = -40 J."
level within, provenance standard, sources [], textbook_note: "Keeps the textbook's W = F·d and F d cos θ; makes the projection reason explicit."

G2:
title: "Effort is not always mechanical work"
content: "In physics, work requires a displacement of the point where the force acts and a force component along that displacement. Holding a 50 N load stationary for 10 s does no mechanical work because d = 0, even though muscles consume chemical energy and produce heat. Pushing a rigid wall with 100 N for 5 s also does no work if the wall does not move. Carrying a 5 kg bag horizontally at constant height: the hand's upward force is about 49 N and the displacement is horizontal, so θ = 90° and the work by that force is 0 J; lifting the bag 1 m does W = mgh = 5 × 9.8 × 1 = 49 J. The correction is: tiredness or effort is not the same as mechanical work; only F·d counts."
level within, standard. textbook_note: "Clarifies the textbook's zero-work conditions in T6 and the skidding-cycle example in T7."

G3:
title: "Why kinetic energy has the factor 1/2"
content: "The factor 1/2 is not arbitrary. For a constant force, v^2 - u^2 = 2as. Multiplying by m/2 gives 1/2 m v^2 - 1/2 m u^2 = mas = Fs. For a variable force, use F = ma = m dv/dt and dW = F dx = m v dv/dt dx = m v dv. Integrating gives K = 1/2 m v^2. Thus kinetic energy is the quantity whose change equals the accumulated work. Example: a 2 kg object accelerated from rest to 3 m/s has K = 1/2 × 2 × 3^2 = 9 J; a 3 N force over 3 m also gives W = 9 J."
level within. standard. textbook_note: "Explains the textbook's motivation from v^2-u^2=2as and the definition K=1/2 mv^2."

G4:
title: "Calculus prerequisite: integral as area and chain rule"
content: "Before variable-force work, review two calculus ideas. First, a definite integral ∫_xi^xf F(x) dx is the signed area under the force-displacement graph. Area above the x-axis is positive, below is negative, and the unit is N m = J. Example: F(x)=2x N from x=0 to 3 m gives ∫0^3 2x dx = [x^2]_0^3 = 9 J. Second, for constant mass, dK/dt = d(1/2 m v^2)/dt = m v dv/dt by the chain rule. Since v = dx/dt, dK/dt = F v when F = ma, so dK = F dx. This is the bridge from power P = F·v to the work-energy theorem."
level within. standard. textbook_note: "Supplies the calculus background used in T10 and T11 without changing the textbook's notation."

G5:
title: "From small-step sum to definite integral"
content: "To see W = ∫ F dx as a method, split the displacement from xi to xf into small pieces Δx_i. Over each small piece, approximate the force as constant: ΔW_i ≈ F(x_i) Δx_i. The total work is the sum Σ F(x_i) Δx_i. As the pieces become smaller and more numerous, the sum approaches the definite integral ∫_xi^xf F(x) dx. The same limiting idea gives dK = F dx for each small step, and summing/integrating gives Kf - Ki = ∫ F dx. Example: for F=2x N from 0 to 3 m, a coarse sum with Δx=1 m gives 2(0.5)(1)+2(1.5)(1)+2(2.5)(1)=10 J; the exact integral is 9 J, and the sum improves as Δx decreases."
level within. standard. textbook_note: "Fills the skipped limiting step in T10 and T11 while keeping the textbook's integral form."

G6:
title: "Meaning of the minus sign in F = -dV/dx"
content: "The minus sign means a conservative force points toward lower potential energy. If V increases with x, dV/dx is positive, so F is negative: the force acts toward decreasing x. For gravity near Earth, take h upward, V(h)=mgh, dV/dh=g, so F_h=-mg, i.e. downward. For a spring, V(x)=1/2 kx^2, dV/dx=kx, so F=-kx, restoring toward x=0. Equivalently, dV = -F dx: when the force and displacement are in the same direction, potential energy decreases; when you move against the force, potential energy increases. Example: lifting a 2 kg mass by 1 m increases V by 19.6 J, while gravity does -19.6 J of work."
level within. standard. textbook_note: "Keeps the textbook's F = -dV/dx and makes the sign physically meaningful for gravity and springs."

G7:
title: "Deriving spring potential energy from variable force"
content: "A spring force is not constant: F_s = -kx. To stretch it slowly from x=0 to x, an external agent applies +kx. The work done by the external agent is the area under the F-x graph, a triangle with base x and height kx: W_ext = 1/2 (kx)(x) = 1/2 kx^2. In integral form, W_ext = ∫_0^x kx' dx' = 1/2 kx^2. The spring force does the negative of this work, so the stored potential energy is V(x)=1/2 kx^2, with V(0)=0. Example: k=200 N/m, x=0.10 m gives V=1/2 × 200 × 0.10^2 = 1.0 J; the average external force is 10 N over 0.10 m, also 1.0 J."
level within. standard. textbook_note: "Fills the skipped average-force/integral step in T16 and keeps the textbook's zero at equilibrium."

G8:
title: "Friction converts mechanical energy, it does not destroy it"
content: "A common misconception is that friction destroys energy. In fact, friction converts mechanical energy into internal thermal energy, sound, and deformation. For a block sliding with a friction force of 5 N over 3 m, W_f = -15 J; the block's kinetic energy decreases by 15 J, and about 15 J appears as heat in the block and surface. In a skidding car, kinetic energy becomes heat in tires and road. In an inelastic collision, the decrease in kinetic energy becomes deformation, heat, and sound. The textbook relation Ef - Ei = W_nc is therefore not a loss of total energy: if W_nc is negative, mechanical energy decreases, but total energy including thermal energy is conserved."
level within. standard. textbook_note: "Refines T14 and T18 by distinguishing mechanical energy from total energy while keeping Ef - Ei = W_nc."

G9:
title: "Relative-speed relation in 1D elastic collisions"
content: "The algebraic key is that for a 1D elastic collision the relative speed reverses: v1i - v2i = v2f - v1f, or v1i - v2i = -(v1f - v2f). This follows from combining momentum conservation with kinetic-energy conservation. If m2 is initially at rest, v2i=0, so v1i = v2f - v1f. Combine this with momentum conservation m1 v1i = m1 v1f + m2 v2f to solve linearly: v1f = ((m1 - m2)/(m1 + m2)) v1i and v2f = (2m1/(m1 + m2)) v1i. Example: equal masses, v1i=4 m/s, v2i=0 gives v1f=0 and v2f=4 m/s; the moving ball stops and the stationary ball moves off with the original speed."
level within. standard. textbook_note: "Supplies the missing intermediate relation in T22 and keeps the textbook's final formulas."

G10:
title: "Vector-triangle picture for equal-mass glancing collisions"
content: "For two equal masses with one initially at rest, momentum conservation gives m v_i = m v1f + m v2f, so v_i = v1f + v2f as a vector equation. Elastic energy conservation gives 1/2 m v_i^2 = 1/2 m v1f^2 + 1/2 m v2f^2, so v_i^2 = v1f^2 + v2f^2. These two equations say that the two final velocity vectors are the legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the initial velocity vector. Therefore v1f and v2f are perpendicular. A useful drawing is: draw the initial momentum as the hypotenuse, then draw the two final momenta as the two sides meeting at a right angle. If one final direction is θ, the other is 90° - θ in the equal-mass, one-at-rest case."
level within. standard. textbook_note: "Adds a visual interpretation to the algebraic proof in T25 and the 2D equations in T24."

G11:
title: "Real crash context for the car-spring model"
content: "The textbook car-spring example is an ideal Hooke's-law model: the force is linear, the energy is stored elastically, and the car can rebound. A real frontal crash is different. A 1500 kg car at 50 km/h has speed 13.9 m/s and kinetic energy K = 1/2 m v^2 ≈ 1.45 × 10^5 J = 145 kJ. In a full frontal crash, essentially all of this energy must be dissipated. Crumple zones are the primary absorbers; a commonly cited conservative figure is that the front crumple zone absorbs about 25% of the impact energy, about 36 kJ at 50 km/h, though the actual share can be higher depending on vehicle design. The NHTSA full-frontal rigid-barrier test at 35 mph, about 56 km/h, corresponds to about 181 kJ for the same 1500 kg car. A real force-displacement curve has a peak force followed by a plateau over a crush distance of roughly 0.5 to 1 m; the work is the area under that curve, and the energy becomes heat and permanent deformation rather than recoverable spring energy. If 36 kJ is absorbed over 0.7 m, the average force associated with that portion is about 50 kN, corresponding to an average deceleration of about 3 to 4 g for that portion; the total crash deceleration depends on all energy-absorbing structures."
level extension. provenance web. sources: NHTSA, Wikipedia, Sun Collision. textbook_note: "Keeps the textbook's ideal spring model and energy-conservation calculation; presents real crash behaviour as an extension and refinement."

G12:
title: "Reactor context for neutron moderation"
content: "The NCERT neutron example is a clean elastic-collision application. In real reactors, fission neutrons are fast, with mean energy about 2 MeV and speed about 20,000 km/s. They must be slowed to thermal energies, about 0.025 eV and 2.2 km/s, because U-235 fission is much more probable with slow neutrons. This is an energy reduction by about 8 × 10^7 and a speed reduction by about 10,000. Light nuclei are effective because in a head-on elastic collision the maximum fraction of the neutron's kinetic energy transferred to a stationary nucleus of mass number A is 4A/(1+A)^2: hydrogen A=1 gives 100%, deuterium A=2 gives about 89%, carbon A=12 gives about 28%, while U-235 gives only about 1.7%. Average slowing requires many collisions: roughly 17 to 18 for hydrogen, 25 to 30 for deuterium, and 90 to 115 for graphite. Common moderators are light water, heavy water, and graphite. Light water is the most common, about 75% of reactors, but ordinary hydrogen absorbs some neutrons, so light-water reactors usually need enriched uranium, about 3.5 to 5% U-235. Heavy water, about 5% of reactors, absorbs fewer neutrons and can use natural uranium, about 0.7% U-235, as in CANDU reactors. Graphite, about 20% of reactors, also has low absorption and can use natural uranium, as in RBMK and Magnox/AGR reactors. The kinetic energy lost by neutrons becomes heat in the moderator and is removed by the coolant."
level extension. provenance web. sources: Wikipedia moderator, Wikipedia temperature, IAEA, World Nuclear. Maybe include NRC? Not used. Omit. textbook_note: "Keeps the NCERT neutron-moderation example; adds reactor design context as an extension."

G13:
title: "Limitation of V = mgh"
content: "The formula V = mgh is the near-Earth, constant-g approximation. It is valid when the height change h is small compared with Earth's radius, so g can be treated as 9.8 m/s^2. Example: a 1 kg mass raised 10 m gains 98 J. For large altitude changes, g decreases with distance from Earth's centre, and the more general gravitational potential energy is U = -GMm/r, which is treated in Chapter 7. For example, at 1000 km above Earth's surface g is noticeably smaller than 9.8 m/s^2, so mgh is no longer a good estimate for a satellite. In this chapter, keep the textbook's mgh for everyday heights and flag it as a local approximation."
level within? It references Chapter 7, within syllabus. I'd mark within. standard. textbook_note: "Keeps the textbook's near-surface V=mgh and explicitly marks its domain of validity."

G14:
title: "Kinetic energy depends on the inertial frame"
content: "Kinetic energy K = 1/2 m v^2 is not an absolute number; it depends on the inertial frame because v depends on the frame. A 1 kg ball moving at 2 m/s in the lab frame has K = 2 J, but in a frame moving with the ball its K = 0. The work-energy theorem remains valid in any inertial frame if the work and kinetic energy are both computed in that same frame. In collision problems, choose one inertial frame, usually the lab frame or the centre-of-mass frame, and use it consistently. Example: for a 1 kg ball at 4 m/s colliding elastically with an identical stationary ball, the lab-frame kinetic energy is 8 J before and after; in the centre-of-mass frame the two balls have speeds 2 m/s before and 2 m/s after, with total kinetic energy 4 J. Mixing frames, for example using lab-frame velocities with centre-of-mass work, gives incorrect energy balances."
level extension. standard. textbook_note: "Does not change the textbook's K=1/2 mv^2; adds a frame-consistency caution for collisions and work-energy calculations."
